root_cause.text: The wave5 VPU remove path cleaned up PM runtime and powered down the hardware before unregistering the V4L2 video devices, leaving polling-mode hrtimer/kthread work able to run and call `wave5_vdi_read_register()` on already powered-off registers.
root_cause.evidence: The patch moves `wave5_vpu_enc_unregister_device()`, `wave5_vpu_dec_unregister_device()`, and `v4l2_device_unregister()` to the start of `wave5_vpu_remove()`, and the commit message states the old order disabled PM runtime first, allowing the hrtimer-driven worker `wave5_vpu_irq_work_fn()` to access hardware registers after autosuspend/power-off, causing a synchronous external abort/kernel panic.

agent_logs.root_cause_candidate: The wave5 VPU remove path cleaned up PM runtime and powered down the hardware before unregistering the V4L2 video devices, leaving polling-mode hrtimer/kthread work able to run and call `wave5_vdi_read_register()` on already powered-off registers.
agent_logs.evidence_points: The patch moves `wave5_vpu_enc_unregister_device()`, `wave5_vpu_dec_unregister_device()`, and `v4l2_device_unregister()` to the start of `wave5_vpu_remove()`, and the commit message states the old order disabled PM runtime first, allowing the hrtimer-driven worker `wave5_vpu_irq_work_fn()` to access hardware registers after autosuspend/power-off, causing a synchronous external abort/kernel panic.

intent_record.intent_summary: Fix device removal cleanup by unregistering VPU encoder/decoder devices and the V4L2 device before shutdown.
intent_record.what: In the platform device remove function, three cleanup calls were added before the existing IRQ check: `wave5_vpu_enc_unregister_device(dev)`, `wave5_vpu_dec_unregister_device(dev)`, and `v4l2_device_unregister(&dev->v4l2_dev)`.
intent_record.how: At device removal time, the driver now explicitly unregisters the VPU encoder and decoder devices and tears down the associated V4L2 device, preventing these subdevices and the V4L2 core from remaining registered after the parent platform device is removed.

intent_record.intent_summary: Remove redundant V4L2 and encoder/decoder unregistration from the remove path to fix cleanup ordering during device teardown.
intent_record.what: In wave5_vpu_remove(), three teardown calls were deleted: wave5_vpu_enc_unregister_device(dev), wave5_vpu_dec_unregister_device(dev), and v4l2_device_unregister(&dev->v4l2_dev). The remaining cleanup sequence now goes directly from clk_bulk_disable_unprepare() to wave5_vdi_release() and ida_destroy().
intent_record.how: At runtime, the driver removal path no longer explicitly unregisters the encoder/decoder devices or the V4L2 device structure. This changes the teardown sequence and may avoid double-unregistering or removing resources that are now handled elsewhere in the device lifecycle.

grouping_result.intent: Fix device removal cleanup by unregistering VPU encoder/decoder devices and the V4L2 device before shutdown.
Remove redundant V4L2 and encoder/decoder unregistration from the remove path to fix cleanup ordering during device teardown.

relevance_review.reason: The root cause is that the driver powered off the hardware before unregistering V4L2 devices, allowing polling work to access registers after shutdown. This change explicitly fixes removal cleanup by unregistering the encoder/decoder and V4L2 devices before shutdown, directly addressing that race.

The change directly affects the device remove/teardown ordering around V4L2 unregistration, which is the same area as the root cause. Reordering or removing unregistration in the remove path is relevant because the bug involved cleanup happening before video devices were fully unregistered, allowing polling work to access powered-off hardware.

candidates.rationale: This appears in the remove path after clocks and resets are already being shut down, so it is part of the teardown sequence that powered off the hardware before video device unregistration, allowing polling work to race with powered-off registers.

The root cause involves polling-mode hrtimer/kthread work still being able to run during removal; this statement is the explicit cleanup of that timer and is directly related to the unsafe ordering in the pre-fix path.

This is the workqueue cancellation for the polling path. If unregister/shutdown happens before all work is fully stopped, the work can still access registers after power-off, matching the reported race.
Disabling clocks is part of the hardware power-down that occurred before V4L2 device unregistration in the vulnerable sequence, creating the window where polling code could still touch registers.
Asserting reset also contributes to powering down the device before video device teardown, which is the ordering flaw described in the root cause.

vuln_statements.explanation: This is in the remove path after clocks/reset teardown, so it participates in the pre-fix ordering where hardware was powered down before V4L2 device unregistration, allowing polling work to race and call into powered-off registers.
Disabling clocks is part of the hardware shutdown that occurred before unregistering the video devices, creating the window where hrtimer/kthread polling could still access registers after power-off.

Asserting reset is part of the power-down sequence that happened before device unregistration in the vulnerable remove path, which left polling-mode work able to run against inaccessible hardware registers.

This cancels the polling timer, and the fix indicates it needed to happen before shutdown; in the vulnerable ordering, the timer could still fire after hardware power-off and reach wave5_vdi_read_register().
This stops the polling workqueue, and the root cause is that this work could still execute during teardown after power-off, leading to register accesses on already disabled hardware.
